bib.title: Enriching Word Vectors with Subword Information
bib.venue: Transactions of the Association for Computational Linguistics, vol. 5, pp. 135-146

read.skipped: References skimmed for lineage only. Figures 1-2 are plots; their values are not in the text.

question: Can word vectors that represent each word as a sum of character n-gram vectors capture morphology and give vectors for unseen words better than one-vector-per-word models?
hypothesis: Using character n-gram information improves vectors for rare words and morphologically rich languages, and makes the model more robust to small training sets.
contributions: An extension of the continuous skipgram model that takes subword information into account (words as sums of character n-gram vectors)
Evaluation on nine languages with different morphologies

method.summary: Skipgram with negative sampling where the word score is the sum of vectors of the word's hashed character n-grams (n from 3 to 6, plus the whole word), dotted with the context vector. Trained on Wikipedia in nine languages and compared with word2vec skipgram and cbow on similarity, analogy and language modelling.
method.task: word embedding pretraining (skipgram with negative sampling plus subword n-grams)

datasets.name: Wikipedia dumps (Arabic, Czech, German, English, Spanish, French, Italian, Romanian, Russian)
datasets.split: 5 passes over shuffled data; for the data-size study the first 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 50 percent (nested subsets, not reshuffled)
datasets.preprocessing: Matt Mahoney's pre-processing perl script; keep words that appear at least 5 times

datasets.name: English Wikipedia of Shaoul and Westbury (2010); WMT 2013 news crawl (DE, ES, FR); Europarl and news commentary (for Botha and Blunsom comparison)
datasets.source: same corpora as the compared methods

datasets.name: Word similarity sets: GUR65, GUR350, ZG222 (DE), WS353 and RW (EN), RG65 (FR), Hassan and Mihalcea 2009 sets (ES, AR, RO), HJ (RU)
datasets.preprocessing: words absent from training get null vectors (sisg-) or n-gram sums (sisg)

datasets.name: Analogy sets (Mikolov 2013a EN; Svoboda and Brychcin 2016 CS; Koper 2015 DE; Berardi 2015 IT)
datasets.preprocessing: questions containing words not in the training corpus excluded

datasets.name: Language modelling data of Botha and Blunsom (2014): CS, DE, ES, FR, RU
datasets.size: roughly one million training tokens each; vocab 46k CS, 37k DE, 27k ES, 25k FR, 63k RU
datasets.split: same preprocessing and splits as Botha and Blunsom (2014)

models.name: sisg (Subword Information Skip Gram)
models.architecture: skipgram with negative sampling, word = sum of character n-gram vectors, dim 300
models.tokenizer: character n-grams n=3..6 with < and > boundary symbols plus the whole word
models.context: window size c sampled uniformly from 1 to 5

models.name: word2vec skipgram (sg) and cbow
models.architecture: C implementation from word2vec package, dim 300

models.name: LSTM language model
models.architecture: recurrent network with 650 LSTM units; lookup table initialised with pre-trained vectors
models.init_from: sg or sisg vectors trained on the LM training set

training.objective: binary logistic loss with negative sampling; score s(w,c) = sum over n-grams g in G_w of z_g^T v_c
training.optimizer: SGD with linear decay of step size gamma0(1 - t/(TP)), Hogwild asynchronous parallel updates
training.lr: gamma0 = 0.025 (skipgram baseline); 0.05 (sisg and cbow baseline). LM: Adagrad lr 0.1
training.lr_schedule: linear decay to zero over T*P steps
training.regularisation: subsampling of frequent words with rejection threshold 1e-4; 5 negatives per positive sampled proportional to square root of unigram frequency; LM gradient clipping at norm 1.0; LM weights initialised in [-0.05, 0.05]

other.speed: 105k words/second/thread for sisg vs 145k for skipgram on English (about 1.5x slower)
other.n-gram_range_choice: 3-6 called arbitrary; no proper validation procedure used

inference.samples: single run per setting; no seeds or variance reported

parameters.oov_vector: sum of the word's n-gram vectors (Sec 5.1); Sec 6.3 says 'average'

metrics.name: Spearman rank correlation
metrics.definition: between human similarity judgement and cosine similarity of vectors

metrics.name: Analogy accuracy
metrics.definition: A is to B as C is to D, predict D; semantic and syntactic reported separately

eval.protocol: No significance tests, seeds or confidence intervals. Results are single numbers rounded to integers.

availability.data: public Wikipedia dumps and cited evaluation sets

evidence.quote: The step size γ0 is set to 0.025 for the skipgram baseline and to 0.05 for both our model and the cbow baseline.

results.claim: sisg beats skipgram and cbow on all word-similarity sets except English WS353, and OOV vectors are never worse than null vectors.
results.setup: German GUR350, Wikipedia dump, 300-d, 5 passes; sisg uses n-gram sums for OOV words
results.table: Table 1, row DE GUR350, columns sg 61, cbow 62, sisg- 64, sisg 70

results.claim: On English rare words (RW) sisg beats both baselines, while on English WS353 (common words) it does not.
results.setup: English Wikipedia, RW dataset; on WS353 sisg 71 vs cbow 73
results.table: Table 1, row EN RW, columns sg 43, cbow 43, sisg- 46, sisg 47

results.claim: Subword information strongly improves syntactic analogies; Czech syntactic accuracy rises from 55.0 (cbow) to 77.8.
results.table: Table 2, row CS Syntactic, columns sg 52.8, cbow 55.0, sisg 77.8

results.claim: Subword information does not help semantic analogies and degrades German (66.5/66.8 to 62.3) and Italian semantic accuracy.
results.table: Table 2, row DE Semantic, columns sg 66.5, cbow 66.8, sisg 62.3
results.note: Authors say the effect is tied to n-gram length and degrades less with an optimal choice (Sec 5.5).

results.claim: With the same training data as the compared methods, sisg beats the morphology-based methods on most sets, for example German GUR350 73 vs 64 (Soricut and Och).
results.setup: German news crawl data (WMT 2013), GUR350; Soricut and Och 2015 baseline
results.table: Table 3, row Soricut and Och (2015) vs next sisg row, column DE GUR350 (64 vs 73)
results.note: The paper says the large German gain is because the baseline does not model noun compounding.

results.claim: A model trained on 5% of Wikipedia beats cbow trained on all of it on German GUR350.
results.setup: sisg on 5% of German Wikipedia vs cbow on 100%, GUR350
results.quote: our model (sisg) trained on 5% of the data achieves better performance (66) than the cbow baseline trained on the full dataset (62)

results.claim: On English RW, 1% of Wikipedia gives sisg 45 against 43 for cbow on the full data.
results.setup: English RW, sisg on 1% of Wikipedia vs cbow on 100%
results.quote: using 1% of the Wikipedia corpus we achieve a correlation coefficient of 45 which is better than the performance of cbow trained on the full dataset (43)

results.claim: Pre-training with sisg vectors lowers LSTM perplexity versus skipgram vectors most for Russian and Czech.
results.setup: Russian LM, about 1M training tokens, 650-unit LSTM, lookup initialised from vectors
results.quote: Czech (8% reduction of perplexity over sg) and Russian (13% reduction)

results.claim: Training is about 1.5x slower than the skipgram baseline.
results.quote: we process 105k words/second/thread versus 145k words/second/thread for the baseline

results.claim: Including n-grams longer than 2 matters; 3-6 works reasonably across languages but was chosen arbitrarily without validation.
results.setup: English RW, n-gram range 3-6 gives 48 vs 41 for range 2-2
results.table: Table 4(d) EN-RW, row i=2 column j=2 is 41; row i=3, column j=6 is 48

limits: Authors concede no proper validation procedure for n-gram ranges due to scarcity of test data; 3-6 was arbitrary (Sec 5.5).
No seeds, variance or significance tests; numbers are integers from single runs.
Subword vectors hurt semantic analogies for German and Italian (Sec 5.2).
Corpus token counts, hardware and total training time are not stated.
Qualitative analyses (Tables 6, 7, Fig 2) use hand-picked examples.
Static word vectors; no context-dependent representations, superseded by contextual models.

terms.definition: Subword Information Skip Gram: the proposed model; sisg- uses null vectors for OOV words, sisg sums n-gram vectors

lineage.work: Distributed representations of words and phrases and their compositionality (skipgram with negative sampling)
lineage.note: Model is derived from continuous skipgram

lineage.work: Efficient estimation of word representations in vector space

lineage.note: Closest earlier idea: summed character four-gram vectors from SVD

lineage.note: Similarity and LM baseline and LM data

Luong et al. 2013; Qiu et al. 2014

figures.caption: Influence of size of the training data on performance (DE-GUR350 and EN-RW, cbow vs sisg- vs sisg)
figures.why: Shows sisg saturates early and beats cbow at small data sizes

figures.why: Shows which n-grams of an OOV word match its partner (micro/circuit, -ness/-ity)
